notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Numbers 6, drawn from the available sources.

---

## Numbers 6:1-21 — The Nazirite Vow

### v. 1: "And the LORD said to Moses"

The chapter opens with a new divine communication to Moses. Gill notes that this law was given immediately after the law concerning the suspected adulteress (ch. 5), and Jewish commentators see a connection: since wine leads to adultery, the Nazirite's abstinence from wine served as a safeguard against unchastity (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm). The Precept Austin outline notes that whereas Numbers 5 dealt with cleansing the camp from the unclean and sinful, Numbers 6 shows how consecration was possible for every Israelite (preceptaustin.org/numbers-6-commentary).

### v. 2: "If a man or woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD"

The Hebrew verb translated "makes a special vow" (*pala*) means "to do something wonderful or extraordinary" — the same word used in Leviticus 27:2 for a "singular vow." Ellicott notes the spiritual lesson: "Christ's servants are expected and required to do something more than others" (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm). Gill remarks that the person taking this vow was doing "something unusual and uncommon," out of step with "the men of the world" (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm). Enduring Word says the vow expressed "one's special desire to draw close to God and to separate oneself from the comforts and pleasures of this world" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

**Women could take the vow.** The Pulpit Commentary calls this "not a little remarkable" because women's religious standing under the law was "markedly inferior," yet here the Spirit's freedom was recognized — "an anticipation of the time when the spirit of self-devotion should be poured out without distinction upon men and women" (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/6.htm).

**The word "Nazirite"** derives from Hebrew *nazir*, meaning "set apart" or "consecrated." Wenham (cited by Enduring Word) notes it is sometimes confused with "Nazarene" (Jesus' hometown designation), but they are distinct words from the same root (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/). Leviticus 25:5, 11 calls untrimmed vines "Nazirites" — a figurative connection to the unshorn hair of the person under vow.

**It was open to all, not just priests.** Enduring Word observes: "The priesthood was restrictive. Only men of a certain age from a very particular family could be priests. The consecration of a Nazirite vow was open to all" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/). Constable agrees: "Complete holiness was not the sole prerogative of the priesthood or the Levites" (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-6.html).

**Catholic view:** Haydock cites Calmet that the custom of cutting hair in honour of a god was common among pagans, and St. Cyril thought Moses permitted it for the true God to divert Israel from superstition. Nazirites for life included Samson and John the Baptist; temporary Nazirites included St. Paul (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-6.html).

### v. 3: "He is to abstain from wine and strong drink… must not drink any grape juice or eat fresh grapes or raisins"

Three aspects of abstinence from grape products are listed. Gill explains that the prohibition moved outward from wine to all grape products as "a kind of hedge, to keep at a distance from drinking wine" (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm). Ellicott notes that the Nazirite's law was stricter than that for priests: priests were forbidden wine only while on tabernacle duty (Leviticus 10:9), but Nazirites were forbidden it entirely. The ban extended even to non-intoxicating grape products, "designed to denote the entire consecration of the Nazirite to the Divine service, and the obligation which rested upon him to abstain from all the desires and delights of the flesh" (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm). He adds that Hosea 3:1 couples "the love of cakes made of raisins" with idolatry.

Enduring Word says: "Generally speaking, wine and grape products were thought to be a blessing (Proverbs 3:10), things to be gratefully received from God (Psalms 104:15)." The Nazirite gave up a legitimate blessing to express special devotion (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

**The term "strong drink" (*shecar*)** is understood by Ellicott as probably made from barley, dates, or honey (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm).

### v. 4: "All the days of his separation, he is not to eat anything that comes from the grapevine, not even the seeds or skins"

The total prohibition — "from the kernels even to the husk" (KJV) — reinforces the comprehensive nature of the abstinence. Ellicott notes the Hebrew words *chartzannim* (sour grapes or kernels) and *zag* (shell or husk) are debated, but the point is clear: the entire grapevine is off-limits (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm). Gill cites a rabbinic debate over which word referred to the outer and which to the inner part of the grape, concluding "it matters not much… since both are forbidden" (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm).

### v. 5: "No razor shall pass over his head… he must let the hair of his head grow long"

The uncut hair was the most publicly visible sign of the vow. Ellicott illustrates by reference to Leviticus 25:4-5, 11: in the sabbatical year the vine was not pruned, and the grapes of the "undressed vine" were literally called "grapes of the Nazirite" — both were left to grow untrimmed (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm).

Gill gives two reasons for the uncut hair: (1) a mystery — letting hair grow signified "an increase of virtue or grace," as Samson's strength increased with his hair; (2) a corrective to pagan practices — taking what the Egyptians used in service of demons and redirecting it to the true God (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm).

Constable (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-6.html) says hair "represented the strength and vitality of the individual" (cf. Judges 16:17; 2 Samuel 14:25-26), so the long hair "symbolized the dedication of the Nazirite's strength and vigor to God."

**Catholic view (Haydock):** Notes that the custom of cutting hair in honour of a god was common among pagans; Moses may have redirected the practice toward the true God (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-6.html).

### vv. 6-7: "He must not go near a dead body… Even if his father or mother or brother or sister should die"

This prohibition equalled the high priest's standard and exceeded that of ordinary priests, who could mourn for close relatives (Leviticus 21:1-3). Ellicott: "The law of the Nazirite in this respect was equally stringent with that of the high priest (Leviticus 21:11)" (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm). Enduring Word calls this "separation from death — the most obvious and terrible consequence of sin" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/). R.D. Cole (cited by Enduring Word) links Jesus' words: "Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead" (Matthew 8:21-22).

The phrase "the crown of consecration to his God is upon his head" (v. 7) — the Hebrew *nezer* can mean both "separation/consecration" and "crown." The Targum of Jonathan renders it "the crown of his God," as noted by Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm). The long hair itself was the visible "crown" of his devotion.

### v. 8: "Throughout the time of his separation, he is holy to the LORD"

A summary statement. Precept Austin emphasizes: "What he abstained from was important but holiness to the LORD was of paramount importance" (preceptaustin.org/numbers-6-commentary). Enduring Word adds there were no additional moral requirements such as abstinence from marital relations — the Nazirite was not called to monasticism but to ordinary life marked by these visible signs (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

### v. 9: "If someone suddenly dies in his presence and defiles his consecrated head of hair, he must shave his head on the day of his cleansing—the seventh day"

This covers accidental defilement. Gill explains that the Nazirite became unclean for seven days (per Numbers 19:11), and shaving the head on the seventh day was part of cleansing. The defiled hair — which was the visible sign of consecration — had to be removed entirely, and the Nazirite would need to start again with new hair growth (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm).

### vv. 10-11: "On the eighth day he must bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons… one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering"

The eighth-day offering mirrors that of the poorer sort of purification rites (cf. Leviticus 12:8; 15:14). Gill notes that even an accidental, involuntary defilement required a sin offering, teaching that "the sins of holy things can be removed in no other way" than by sacrifice — a type of Christ's atonement (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm).

The phrase "he has sinned by being in the presence of the dead body" reflects ceremonial, not moral, guilt. Ellicott explains the Hebrew preposition means "by reason of, or on account of the dead body" (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm). Enduring Word emphasizes: "God required a sacrifice of atonement, a sacrifice of rededication, and the wiping away of the former days of the vow" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

### v. 12: "He must rededicate his time of separation… bring a year-old male lamb as a guilt offering. But the preceding days shall not be counted"

The guilt offering (male lamb) was additional to the sin and burnt offerings. Gill underlines the severity: even if the defilement occurred on the last day of the vow, all prior days were lost and the entire period had to begin again (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm). Enduring Word cites the Mishnah's account that Queen Helena had nearly completed seven years of a Nazirite vow when she was defiled and had to keep it for another seven years (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

### v. 13: "Now this is the law of the Nazirite when his time of separation is complete: He must be brought to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting"

The completion of the vow required an appearance at the sanctuary. Gill notes the passive "he shall be brought" — the Targum of Jonathan says "he shall bring himself," i.e., present himself, but others suggest the priest might bring him if necessary (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm). The Pulpit Commentary observes that the original law contemplated only temporary vows; all biblical Nazirites we read of (Samson, Samuel, John the Baptist) were lifelong, and their vows were made for them before birth (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/6.htm). Hegesippus (cited in Eusebius) reports that James the Lord's brother was also a Nazirite.

### vv. 14-15: The required offerings

The completion offerings were extensive and expensive: an unblemished year-old male lamb (burnt offering), an unblemished year-old female lamb (sin offering), an unblemished ram (peace offering), plus grain offerings, drink offerings, and a basket of unleavened cakes and wafers. Ellicott explains: the sin offering atoned for sins committed during the vow period; the burnt offering "typified the entire consecration of the body, soul, and spirit of the offerer to the Lord"; the peace offering expressed joyful fellowship. The word for "offer" in v. 14 (*hiqriv*, "to bring near") is related to *Corban* — a gift offered to God (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm).

Enduring Word: "This was an expensive vow to fulfill. The Nazirite vow was not something that could be entered into lightly" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/). When Paul visited Jerusalem, he paid the expenses of some Christians completing their Nazirite vows (Acts 21:23-24).

### v. 16: "The priest is to present all these before the LORD and make the sin offering and the burnt offering"

The sin offering was offered first (noted explicitly here, though the burnt offering was listed first in v. 14), then the burnt offering. Gill observes the sin offering always preceded the burnt offering in actual performance, as atonement must precede consecration (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm).

### v. 17: "He shall also offer the ram as a peace offering… along with the basket of unleavened bread"

The peace offering (also called fellowship or well-being offering) provided a meal that the Nazirite and his friends could share. Gill remarks: the burnt offering was wholly the Lord's, the sin offering gave a portion to the priest, and the peace offerings gave a share to the Nazirite and his friends — "everyone had their share" (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/6.htm).

### v. 18: "Then at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, the Nazirite is to shave his consecrated head, take the hair, and put it on the fire under the peace offering"

This was the climactic public act. The hair — the visible symbol of the Nazirite's consecration throughout the vow — was shaved and placed on the altar fire beneath the peace offering. Ellicott calls this "a solemn and suitable termination of the days of his separation to the Lord" (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm). Constable says it "probably symbolized giving to God the strength and vigor that he had previously employed in His service" and also ensured that "no one would misuse his hair, possibly in a pagan ritual" (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-6.html).

### vv. 19-20: "The priest is to take the boiled shoulder… one unleavened cake… one unleavened wafer, and put them into the hands of the Nazirite… The priest shall then wave them as a wave offering"

The boiled shoulder of the ram, along with bread from the basket, was placed in the Nazirite's hands, and the priest waved them together (or perhaps took them back and waved them). This was the "wave offering" (*tenuphah*). These portions became "a holy portion for the priest," along with the breast and thigh that were the priest's normal share of peace offerings. Enduring Word notes "the active participation of the Nazirite in this ceremony" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

The final phrase — "After that, the Nazirite may drink wine" — marks the official end of the vow's restrictions.

### v. 21: "This is the law of the Nazirite… in addition to whatever else he can afford; he must fulfill whatever vow he makes"

A concluding summary. Ellicott: "besides any voluntary offerings which it may be in his power to make" (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm). The vow was binding; once made, it had to be fulfilled according to the law. The provision "whatever else he can afford" allowed for generosity beyond the minimum requirement.

**Catholic view (Haydock):** Notes that Nazirite vows generally lasted a month and were to be performed at Jerusalem; girls could not bind themselves before age ten and a day, boys before thirteen. Josephus records that Hebrews made such vows when attacked by dangerous illness (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-6.html).

## Numbers 6:22-27 — The Priestly (Aaronic) Blessing

### vv. 22-23: "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Tell Aaron and his sons: This is how you are to bless the Israelites'"

The blessing was dictated word-for-word by God; the priests were not free to improvise. Spurgeon (cited by Enduring Word): "The children of Israel might miss blessing through the ignorance, or forgetfulness, or unbelief of Aaron; and therefore it was not left to him; but he had to learn by heart each word and sentence… if God himself puts the very words into the mouth of his priest, then they are God's words" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

**The placement after the Nazirite section is intentional.** Enduring Word: "Whenever there is some special act to demonstrate consecration… we easily think that these specially separated people are the ones — perhaps the only ones — whom God wants to bless. We need to be reminded that… God loves to bless His people, and blesses them far more freely than they usually imagine" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

**Reformed:** Ligonier notes that the Aaronic benediction was "inaugurated during Israel's wilderness experience" as "a divine word of promise and blessing" assuring Israel God would be with them through the wilderness. It was "ultimately realized in the person and redemptive work of Christ" — "only through faith in Jesus, the final High Priest and sacrificial Lamb, do sinners truly know the amazing blessing" (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gospel-benediction). Calvin called it "an efficacious testimony of God's grace."

**Lutheran:** The LCMS notes that Luther brought the priestly blessing to prominence in the Divine Service through his *Formula Missae* (1523). Luther saw three key ideas: "forgiveness, the sun, and the word. The blessing speaks directly of the forgiveness of sins. When the believer experiences God's forgiveness, it is like the shining of the sun bringing joy and brightness" (resources.lcms.org/reading-study/commentaries/pastoral-blessing-and-the-benediction/). Lutheran practice includes the pastor speaking the benediction with uplifted hands and making the sign of the cross, "saying the Old Testament words are effective because of God's peacemaking on the cross."

### v. 24: "May the LORD bless you and keep you"

The first couplet. "Bless" is comprehensive — all good from God. "Keep" (*shamar*) means to guard, protect, preserve. Ligonier: "To bless is to keep" — the second half of each verse "accents the meaning of the first" (learn.ligonier.org/articles/may-lord-bless-you-and-keep-you). Enduring Word: "Some are kept by their own sin and desire, some are kept by idolatry and greed… But to be kept by the LORD ensures life, peace, and success" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

**Reformed (Spurgeon via Enduring Word):** The blessing is for those "resting upon Christ." Spurgeon: "'Oh! but I do not deserve it.' Just so; but 'the Lord Bless thee.' 'I am so unworthy, I am so backsliding.' Yes, but the Lord Jesus Christ knows all, covers all" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

**Baptist (Desiring God):** The Expositor's Bible Commentary notes this first couplet invokes "the providential care and favour of God, as Ruler of the universe, Arbiter among the nations, Source of creaturely life, Upholder of human existence" — expanded in Psalm 121 (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-6.html).

### v. 25: "May the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you"

The second couplet. God's "face shining" is an image of favour, delight, and approval. Ligonier: "To know that as God looks upon you, He is well pleased — not because of who you are, or what you have done, but because you are in Jesus Christ — there is no greater source of peace and power in life" (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/aaronic-blessing). Calvin wrote that "nothing is more desirable for the consummation of our happiness, than that we should behold the serene countenance of God."

Spurgeon (cited by Enduring Word): "Why should he fret when God smiles? What matters though all the world should censure, if Jehovah countenances his servant. A look of approval from God creates a deep, delightful calm within the soul" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

**Reformed (Ligonier):** The Aaronic blessing expresses "the hope that the Lord's chosen will one day see His face. Our supreme longing is to experience the beatific vision — to see the Lord face-to-face as He shines His smile upon us" (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/aaronic-blessing).

### v. 26: "May the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace"

The third couplet. "Lift up His countenance" means to pay favourable attention, to look upon with love. Wenham (cited by Enduring Word): "When God smiles on his people, they can be sure that he will be gracious to them" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

"Peace" (*shalom*) is far more than cessation of conflict. Enduring Word: "This peace, this shalom is God's word for wholeness and goodness and total satisfaction in life. This is the abundant life Jesus promised (John 10:10)" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/). The Expositor's Bible Commentary notes the three couplets — Preservation, Enlightenment, Peace — "bear a relation, by no means fanciful, to the work of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit" (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-6.html).

**The threefold repetition of "the LORD" (Yahweh):** Ellicott says "there has been commonly recognised in this blessing an allusion to the doctrine of the Trinity" (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm). Spurgeon: "I will not say that this teaches the doctrine of the Trinity; but I must say that, believing the doctrine of the Trinity, I understand the passage all the better. The shadow of the Triune God is on the sacred benediction in the name thrice repeated" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/). Structurally, Ligonier notes that removing the three instances of "Yahweh" leaves twelve Hebrew words — an intentional reference to the twelve tribes (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/aaronic-blessing).

**The sixfold "you":** Each line addresses "you" — the individual within the covenant community. Enduring Word: "We often feel as if God really wants to bless someone else. He wants to bless us" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

### v. 27: "So they shall put My name on the Israelites, and I will bless them"

The blessing is God placing His covenant name (Yahweh) upon His people. Ligonier: "To invoke the covenantal name of Yahweh is a constant reminder to the people of God of their salvation in Him… Yahweh's blessing is the gift of His name to His people, and it is signed with His own blood" (learn.ligonier.org/articles/may-lord-bless-you-and-keep-you). The blessing marks them as His possession and confers what it declares: "I will bless them" is God's own sure promise.

Enduring Word: "When God saith, 'I will,' all the devils in hell cannot turn aside the blessing, and all the ages of eternity cannot change the King's word" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

**Archaeological note (Enduring Word, citing Cole):** In 1979, excavations at Ketef Hinnom near Jerusalem uncovered two small silver scrolls (late 7th–6th century BC) containing versions of the priestly blessing — the oldest attestation of the Tetragrammaton found in Jerusalem, confirming the antiquity of the benediction (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/).

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Perspectives

| Topic | Reformed (Ligonier) | Lutheran (LCMS) | Baptist (Spurgeon/Gill) | Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word) |
|-------|---------------------|------------------|-------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Aaronic Blessing | An "efficacious testimony of God's grace" (Calvin); realized in Christ; points to beatific vision | God's forgiveness like sunshine; spoken with uplifted hands and sign of the cross; central in liturgy since Luther | Spurgeon: blessing freely given despite unworthiness; received by faith in Christ | Emphasizes personal "you" — God wants to bless each believer; blessing is not earned by acts of consecration |
| Trinity in vv.24-26 | Threefold YHWH is a "shadow" of the Trinity (Spurgeon, cited favorably) | Luther connected the blessing to forgiveness, sun (Christ), and word | Same threefold allusion noted | "The repetition… does not prove the Trinity, but it illustrates it" |
| Nazirite vow | Not specifically addressed in retrieved materials | Not specifically addressed | Gill: typifies Christ and believers' separation; rabbinic details extensively noted | Emphasizes it was open to all, not just priests; a voluntary, extraordinary devotion |

---

## Other Views

**Catholic (Haydock, via StudyLight):** The Nazirite vow is understood as a practice to "acquire greater sanctity and perfection." The Septuagint rendering "whoever has made a great vow to be very pure to the Lord" captures the sense. Haydock notes the practice was also known among pagans (cutting hair for gods), and Moses may have redirected it. Temporary Nazirite vows generally lasted 30 days and were performed at Jerusalem. Age minimums applied: ten years and a day for girls, thirteen for boys. Josephus records vows made during dangerous illness (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-6.html).

**Modern/Critical Scholarship (Peake's Commentary, via StudyLight):** Peake suggests the abstinence from wine may have originated because the vine was associated with Canaanite Baal-worship (cf. Hosea 2:5, 8); to strict Yahweh-worshippers, using vineyard products might seem like "secession from the cult of the God of Israel." The uncut hair reflects "the belief that the hair… was in a special degree the seat of Divine energy" (cf. Judges 16:17). Parallels are cited with the Roman *flamen dialis*, who also could not walk under a vine or touch a dead body. Peake notes that lifelong Nazirites like Samson could not have observed the corpse-avoidance rule (Judges 14:19; 15:8, 15), so the regulations in Numbers 6 applied only to temporary Nazirites (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/numbers-6.html).

**Distinction from Monasticism:** Multiple sources emphasize that the Nazirite was not a monk. Enduring Word (citing Morgan): "There was absolutely nothing monastic in this order. These men did not separate themselves from the ordinary life of their fellows" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-6/). The Pulpit Commentary agrees: "The ideal of this separation… was not that of a life of monastic seclusion, but of action, and of uninterrupted devotion to the Divine service" (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/6.htm).
